claims.text: In as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films or nanoribbons, thermal boundary resistance at the substrate/film interface primarily governs low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
Rapid interfacial heat removal balances magnetic-ordering kinetics with thermal dissipation.
Rapid interfacial heat removal produces narrower hysteresis and a faster thermal response.
Poor interfacial heat transfer delays thermal equilibration, broadens hysteresis, and reduces effective magnetocaloric performance.
Sapphire and glass substrates provide contrasting high and low thermal conductivities, respectively.
Changing the substrate from glass to sapphire will alter the substrate/film thermal boundary conductance.
Thermal boundary conductance determines the rate at which heat is removed during a magnetic-cooling cycle.
Higher interfacial thermal conductance accelerates heat removal.
Accelerated heat removal allows the magnetic state to reverse more rapidly and thereby minimizes hysteresis.
Lower interfacial thermal conductance causes thermal-equilibration lag and increased magnetocaloric-cycle hysteresis.
Relative to the baseline, films on high-thermal-conductivity substrates will have narrower hysteresis loops.
Films on high-thermal-conductivity substrates may exhibit a more pronounced entropy change per cycle and a more reversible magnetocaloric response.
Films on low-thermal-conductivity substrates will exhibit broader hysteresis and thermal lag that limits cycle frequency.
The proposed mechanism applies near the alloy's magnetic-ordering temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies in nanoscale geometries and frequency regimes where cross-interface heat transfer is rate-limiting.
Grain boundaries and crystallinity could modify the observed magnetic or magnetocaloric behavior.
A lack of systematic substrate-dependent change in both hysteresis width and thermal-response rate would falsify the claim that interfacial thermal conductance governs the behavior.
